title: Mastema
lead: Mastema is the leader of the evil spirits in Jubilees, the one who asks God to leave him a tenth of the demons after the Flood, proposes Abraham's test and attacks Moses. The name comes from a Hebrew word for "hostility," from the same root as the Hebrew word satan, and Jubilees treats him as Satan.

sections.b: The Hebrew noun masṭemah, "hostility," occurs in the Bible in Hosea 9:7-8 ("so great the hostility"). R. H. Charles explained it as formed from the same root as satan, "accuse, oppose," and so "the equivalent of the Satan in point of meaning and derivation." The Latin of Jubilees has Mastima; the Greek chroniclers Syncellus and Cedrenus write Mastipham and Mastiphat, and Syncellus calls him "the ruler of the demons." Charles reports Rönsch's remark that outside the Jubilees literature the word is found as a proper noun only in the Acts of Philip ("Mansemat, that is the Satan").

In Jubilees his spirits lead people astray and blind them, accuse them, and destroy those who sin. Charles lists the passages: Mastema asks for a tenth of the spirits (Jubilees 10:8-11), proposes that God test Abraham (Jubilees 17:16), seeks to harm Moses on his way to Egypt (Jubilees 48:2), stands against Moses before Pharaoh (Jubilees 48:9), and "all the powers of Mastema" are sent to kill the firstborn of Egypt (Jubilees 49:2). Yet he acts only within limits God sets. Israel, Charles notes, is God's own portion and not ruled by any spirit (Jubilees 15:32).
sections.refs: Jubilees 10:8-11; Jubilees 17:16; Jubilees 48:2; Jubilees 49:2; Exodus 4:24-26; Job 1:6-12

sections.b: The figure is close to the accuser of Job 1-2, who comes before God and acts only by his leave, and to "the ruler of the demons" of the Gospels (Mark 3:22). Jubilees itself names him Satan (Jubilees 10:11). Where Genesis 22:1 says "God tested Abraham" and Exodus 4:24 says the LORD sought to kill Moses, Jubilees puts Mastema in the hostile role.
